paper_context.research_question: Can a dependency parser for Singlish be built by creating a Universal Dependencies-conformant Singlish treebank and transferring English syntactic knowledge via neural stacking to improve POS tagging and dependency parsing performance?
contribution_type: method application/transfer (neural stacking for cross-lingual transfer)
empirical evaluation (parsing/POS results and error analysis)
contribution_style: engineering of neural models (POS tagger and dependency parser) using existing architectures with transfer
quantitative experimental comparison and error analysis
main_claims: A Singlish dependency treebank of 1,200 annotated sentences (10,986 words) under the Universal Dependencies scheme is created and can represent Singlish-specific constructions within UD labels.
Integrating English syntactic knowledge via feature-level neural stacking substantially improves Singlish POS tagging and dependency parsing compared to training on the small Singlish treebank alone.
Neural stacking yields a parser achieving ~84.21% UAS for Singlish, corresponding to a large relative error reduction (~36.5%) over the baseline Singlish parser.
Singlish-specific word embeddings (ICE-SIN) are more helpful than similarly-sized English embeddings, indicating distributional differences between Singlish and English vocabularies.

The proposed annotation choices (e.g., treatment of discourse particles, topic-prominence, copula deletion, NP deletion) are compatible with UD and allow meaningful analysis of parsing errors by grammar type.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: annotation quality: inter-annotator agreement, UD compliance, coverage of Singlish phenomena
dataset representativeness: selection procedure, domain (forum) coverage, OOV and borrowed-vocabulary handling
modeling validity: clarity of neural stacking integration, hyperparameter choices, use of POS features
empirical performance: POS accuracy, UAS/LAS on held-out test set, comparison to baselines (ENG-on-SIN, base Singlish)
ablation and analysis: effect of different word embeddings, contribution of English knowledge, per-grammar error analysis
reproducibility and release: availability and usability of treebank, code, and trained models
limitations: dataset size, domain bias, potential annotation ambiguities for creole-specific constructions

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper builds a Singlish UD treebank (1,200 sentences) and uses feature-level neural stacking to transfer English POS and syntactic knowledge into Singlish POS tagger and dependency parser. The argument chain: (1) Singlish diverges from English lexically and grammatically -> motivates building a UD-conformant Singlish treebank; (2) English UD-Eng contains large-scale syntactic knowledge that can help low-resource Singlish; (3) neural stacking (concatenating English model features into Singlish models) is an effective transfer mechanism; (4) specialized Singlish embeddings (ICE-SIN) capture distributional patterns absent in English embeddings and further improve performance; (5) together, treebank + stacking + ICE-SIN yield substantial relative error reductions for POS and parsing (reported POS 84.79%, parser UAS 84.21%). The manuscript generally maintains continuity between dataset creation, annotation decisions, model architecture, and experiments. Weaknesses in the chain arise from limited annotation validation (100 double-annotated sentences), small held-out test set (150 sentences), incomplete reporting of some baseline numbers in the text (reliance on tables), and potential confounding between embedding/domain-size and language-specific effects. The core coherence holds: each methodological choice is motivated by earlier claims, but robustness of empirical claims depends on additional ablations, variance estimates, and fuller release/metadata.
logical_argument_graph: A1 Data need: Singlish differs from English (lexically + grammatically) -> off-the-shelf English NLP tools fail on Singlish -> need a Singlish treebank (claims C1).

A2 Resource creation: Build 1,200-sentence Singlish UD treebank using UD-Eng conventions, with specific mapping decisions for topic-prominence, copula/NP deletion, discourse particles -> result: treebank fits UD (C1, C5).
A3 Transfer rationale: English UD-Eng is a suitable source because of shared ancestry and domain similarity -> its learned features can help Singlish parsing (assumption A3).
A4 Method: Use feature-level neural stacking to inject English tagger/parser hidden features into Singlish POS/tagger and parser models (A4).
A5 POS pipeline: Improved POS tagging via stacking (Stack-ICE-SIN) -> better POS predictions used as parser inputs (A5) (claim C2).
A6 Parser pipeline: Base Singlish parser (Dozat & Manning) improved by stacking English parser features -> reported UAS/LAS gains and large relative error reduction (claim C3).
A7 Lexical modeling: ICE-SIN embeddings capture Singlish-specific distributional semantics and outperform matched-size English embeddings, contributing to parsing gains (claim C4).
A8 Evaluation: Per-grammar error analysis shows stacking improves most Singlish constructions, supporting annotation choices and compatibility with UD (claim C5).

A9 Release & reproducibility: Authors state public release of treebank, code, and model (claim C7) -> necessary for validating annotation mappings, reproducing stacking, and checking numerical robustness.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper creates a 1,200-sentence Singlish UD treebank and trains biaffine neural parsers/taggers. To compensate for the small target treebank, the authors transfer English syntactic knowledge via feature-level neural stacking (concatenating English tagger/parser hidden representations into Singlish models) and report substantial relative error reductions on POS tagging (~31.6%) and dependency parsing (~36.5%), achieving 84.21% UAS. They also compare embeddings, reporting that in-domain ICE-SIN embeddings outperform similarly-sized English embeddings. Key methodological dependencies: (i) annotation choices mapping Singlish phenomena into UD-English conventions, (ii) representativeness and size of the dataset and evaluation split (150-sentence test), (iii) design and training parity of baseline vs stacked models, (iv) jackknifing procedures for POS features in parser training, and (v) controls for embedding corpus-size and domain. The paper releases resources but the repository link is anonymized in the manuscript. Overall, the reported gains are plausible given neural stacking, but several assumptions and evaluation choices need clearer evidence to establish robustness and reproducibility.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript constructs a 1,200-sentence Singlish UD-conformant dependency treebank and trains a neural dependency parser that integrates English syntactic knowledge via feature-level neural stacking. The authors (1) justify adopting UD and English UD conventions for Singlish annotation, (2) select forum data emphasizing non-English LM likelihood to collect Singlish instances, (3) annotate and report a 100-sentence inter-annotator UAS/LAS check, (4) implement POS and dependency models based on bi-LSTM-CRF and biaffine parsers respectively, (5) apply neural stacking to incorporate English tagger/parser hidden features into Singlish models, and (6) show empirical gains: POS accuracy from ~77.8% to 84.79% (stacking) and parser UAS to 84.21% (~36.5% relative error reduction). They also compare embeddings (ICE-SIN vs English Giga100M/GloVe) and perform grammar-type error analyses. The paper's reasoning chain: small in-domain Singlish treebank alone is insufficient; English resources contain transferable syntactic signals; neural stacking can inject those signals at the feature level without overwhelming Singlish-specific distributions; combined with Singlish embeddings the stacked model yields substantial empirical improvements. The contribution is incremental: it packages known components (UD annotation, biaffine parser, neural stacking) for a creole and provides a focused empirical evaluation plus a released resource and models.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Off-the-shelf English NLP tools perform poorly on Singlish because of lexical and syntactic divergences.
Resource creation: Build a Singlish UD treebank (1,200 sentences) using UD-Eng conventions with specific mapping rules for Singlish phenomena.
Modeling baseline: Train Singlish POS tagger and dependency parser on the small treebank (bi-LSTM-CRF for POS; biaffine attention parser for dependency).
Transfer hypothesis: English UD resources contain useful syntactic representations that can transfer to Singlish despite lexical differences.
Transfer mechanism: Use feature-level neural stacking to concatenate English tagger/parser hidden features into Singlish model inputs and jointly train/ fine-tune.
Lexical hypothesis: In-domain Singlish embeddings (ICE-SIN) better capture distributional semantics for Singlish tokens than English embeddings, which affects parsing.
Empirical test: Compare baseline, ENG-on-SIN, embedding variants, and stacked models on held-out Singlish test set and per-grammar categories.
Conclusion: Neural stacking plus ICE-SIN yields substantial POS and parsing improvements; UD can represent Singlish phenomena sufficiently for this pipeline; resources and code are released.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper constructs a Universal Dependencies-conformant Singlish treebank (1,200 sentences, 10,986 words), adapts UD/UD-Eng annotation decisions to encode Singlish phenomena, and trains neural POS and dependency models. The core modeling move is feature-level neural stacking: vectors (emission/hidden/MLP features) from an English UD-trained tagger/parser are concatenated into target Singlish models, and the combined network is trained end-to-end so English syntactic knowledge can inform Singlish parsing without full retraining on English data. The authors also compare word embeddings (large English GloVe6B, small English Giga100M, and in-domain ICE-SIN) to probe lexical distribution effects. Empirical claims are that stacking yields substantial relative error reductions for POS tagging (~31.6%) and parsing (~36.5%), producing a parser with ~84.2% UAS, and that ICE-SIN embeddings outperform English embeddings despite smaller corpus size. Annotation choices map diverse Singlish grammars onto existing UD labels (e.g., discourse particles -> INTJ + discourse relation). The evaluation uses train/dev/test splits (900/150/150 sentences), jackknifed POS for training the parser, and per-grammar error analysis. The paper releases data and code (link anonymized in draft).
logical_argument_graph: A: Singlish differs from standard English lexically and syntactically (Leimgruber 2009/2011) -> motivates building a Singlish treebank.
B: UD provides interoperable annotation conventions and UD-Eng is a suitable source -> adopt UD for Singlish and facilitate transfer.
C: English resources are large but Singlish treebank is small -> directly training on Singlish yields low performance; transfer can help.
D: Neural stacking can transfer feature-level syntactic information from English tagger/parser into Singlish models without overwriting Singlish-specific representations.
E: In-domain lexical embeddings (ICE-SIN) capture Singlish distributional semantics better than English embeddings of comparable size -> improved parsing.
F: Empirical results (POS + Parser) show stacking + ICE-SIN yield large relative error reductions -> supports claim that transfer + in-domain embeddings produce state-of-the-art Singlish parsing.
G: Annotation decisions showing UD compatibility + per-grammar error analysis indicate practical usability of the treebank for linguistic analysis and parser error attribution.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a small Universal Dependencies (UD)-conformant Singlish dependency treebank (1,200 sentences, 10,986 words) and applies feature-level neural stacking to transfer English POS and syntactic knowledge (from UD-Eng) into Singlish POS tagger and biaffine dependency parser. The architecture concatenates English tagger/parser hidden features into Singlish models and is trained end-to-end; POS predictions are jackknifed for parser training. Experiments compare embedding sources (ICE-SIN, Giga100M, GloVe6B), and evaluate on a held-out test set (150 sentences). Reported outcomes: Stack-ICE-SIN yields POS accuracy 84.79% (31.6% relative error reduction vs Singlish-only tagger) and parser UAS 84.21% (36.5% relative error reduction vs baseline Singlish parser). The authors argue UD can represent Singlish phenomena via specific mapping choices, that ICE-SIN embeddings capture distributional differences important for parsing, and they release treebank and code (anonymized link in paper). Evidence in manuscript supports these claims at face value, but key uncertainties remain: small train/dev/test sizes (150 test sentences), limited inter-annotator assessment (100 sentences), incomplete reporting of variance/significance and some baseline parity details, and anonymized release link preventing immediate reproducibility checks. Overall, the reasoning chain is coherent—resource creation enables in-domain modeling, English provides transferable syntactic signals, neural stacking injects these signals and improves performance—yet robustness and effect attribution require additional ablations, confidence intervals, and provenance of released artifacts.

If English UD-Eng domain matched the target forum domain more closely (web forum English), transfer might be more effective; conversely, if English UD-Eng diverged, negative transfer could appear.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Neural stacking and biaffine parsers are established methods; their application as feature-level transfer for a creole is a logical adaptation rather than a methodological breakthrough.

uncertainty_flags: No statistical tests or resampling; small sample sizes.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident the paper's central claims are supported in direction (neural stacking + in-domain embeddings improve Singlish parsing) given the provided evidence and established prior methods, but the magnitude and robustness of reported gains are uncertain due to small test and validation sizes, limited ablations, and unverifiable release artifacts. Hence a mid-to-high confidence interval (0.4–0.9) captures substantive support tempered by methodological uncertainties.

consensus_findings: A Singlish UD-conformant dependency treebank of 1,200 sentences (10,986 words) was created and described, with explicit annotation choices for Singlish phenomena (topic-prominence, discourse particles, copula/NP deletion).

Feature-level neural stacking (injecting English tagger/parser hidden features into Singlish models) was implemented and reported to improve both POS tagging and dependency parsing versus training on the small Singlish treebank alone.
In-domain Singlish embeddings (ICE-SIN) produce larger empirical improvements than the English embeddings tested, suggesting distributional/coverage differences matter for parsing performance.
The manuscript documents architecture choices (bi-LSTM-CRF POS tagger, biaffine parser, stacking points) and commits to releasing the treebank, code, and trained models.
Authors provide per-phenomenon (grammar-type) error analyses showing differential gains across Topic Prominence, Copula Deletion, NP Deletion, Discourse Particles and Others.
disagreements: Magnitude and robustness of reported improvements: reviewers agree improvements were reported but disagree on how reliable the point estimates are given the small test set (150 sentences) and lack of confidence intervals; some treat the gains as plausible and meaningful, others urge that they may be sample-noise inflated.

Interpretation of ICE-SIN superiority: some reviewers attribute gains to true language-specific distributional advantages of ICE-SIN, while others argue domain/size/preprocessing confounds could explain the advantage and request controlled embedding experiments.

Attribution of gains to neural stacking per se: reviewers differ on whether stacking is the primary causal mechanism (transferred syntactic signal) versus other explanations (increased model capacity, initialization effects, auxiliary supervision); several call for targeted ablations to resolve this.

Sufficiency of annotation validation: reviewers concur that a treebank exists but differ on acceptability of the validation (100-sentence double-annotation). Some consider the reported IAA figures informative but insufficient; others mark this as a major gap requiring per-phenomenon agreement and adjudication logs.
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical stability of metrics: small held-out test (150 sentences, ~1,381 words) and no bootstrap/CIs or repeated runs increase uncertainty about UAS/LAS/POS effect sizes and statistical significance.

Annotation reliability for Singlish-specific constructions: only 100 sentences double-annotated with aggregate UAS/LAS; per-label and per-phenomenon agreement not reported, leaving open potential annotation inconsistency for the most linguistically distinctive cases.

Embedding comparison confounds: ICE-SIN vs English baselines may be confounded by corpus domain, register, size, or preprocessing differences; current evidence does not isolate 'language' from 'domain/coverage'.

Attribution of stacking benefits: lack of ablations (tagger-only vs parser-only stacking, freeze vs fine-tune, matched-capacity controls) creates ambiguity about which stacked features and training choices drive gains.

Reproducibility and artifact completeness: repository link anonymized in the manuscript; contents, license, annotation guidelines, adjudication logs, and seeds/hyperparameter files are not verifiable from the paper text.
model_diversity_effects: Using an English UD-Eng source model plus feature-level stacking appears to supply complementary syntactic signals that the Singlish models lack when trained on limited data, producing aggregate performance gains across reviewers' experiments.

In-domain lexical representations (ICE-SIN) interact with stacking: reviewers note that embedding coverage and domain match amplify or moderate transfer benefits; thus model improvements arise from both representational (embeddings) and structural (stacking) changes rather than a single factor.

Different reviewers highlighted possible role of model capacity and initialization (e.g., initialized scoring tensor from English parser, larger concatenated inputs) — these engineering effects can mimic or augment transfer benefits and need to be disentangled with controlled experiments.

Jackknifed POS features and joint/backpropagated training enable pipeline synergy: several reviewers observe that improvements in POS tagging plausibly propagate to parsing accuracy, making POS-model design choices an important moderating factor in final parser performance.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the manuscript as a coherent empirical package with a valuable resource contribution and plausible transfer results, but foreground robustness and reproducibility checks in editorial requirements. Request that the authors (1) provide a reproducibility artifact checklist (public repository URL, CoNLL-U files, full annotation guidelines, adjudication logs, train/dev/test splits, preprocessing scripts, random seeds, hyperparameter configs, and license), (2) add statistical robustness analyses (bootstrap confidence intervals for POS/UAS/LAS, or k-fold/Monte Carlo resampling; report absolute error counts), and (3) include targeted ablations to isolate causal components (stacking ablations: tagger-only, parser-only, freezing vs fine-tuning English weights; matched-capacity control for baseline). Emphasize that the editor/wider readership will need per-phenomenon inter-annotator agreement and documentation of ethical/legal constraints for forum-derived data before relying on the released corpus.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and address reviewer concerns, provide: (A) complete public release of artifacts (CoNLL-U annotations, full annotation guidelines, adjudication logs for contested examples, a manifest listing files and licenses); (B) statistical robustness evidence: bootstrap CIs for reported metrics, repeated runs with different seeds, and absolute error counts used to compute relative reductions; (C) ablation studies isolating stacking effects (stack tagger-only vs parser-only features, freeze vs fine-tune English components, matched-capacity baseline that adds similar parameter count without English features); (D) controlled embedding comparisons (train English embeddings on matched-size, matched-domain forum English or downsample ICE-SIN) plus reporting OOV rates and qualitative nearest-neighbor checks for key Singlish tokens; (E) per-label and per-phenomenon inter-annotator agreement scores and examples of common disagreements and adjudication outcomes; and (F) clear statement of dataset licensing, scraping consent/ethics handling, and any usage restrictions.
transparency_report: Manuscript documents high-level architectures, references open-source prior implementations (Chen et al., Dozat & Manning) and lists many hyperparameters, but does not include full experiment scripts, random seeds or per-condition hyperparameter tables in the text.

Repository link is anonymized in the submitted manuscript, preventing verification of released artifacts (annotation files, guidelines, training scripts, pre-trained embeddings, model checkpoints, and license).

Inter-annotator agreement is reported in aggregate for 100 sentences (UAS 85.30%, LAS 75.72%) but lacks per-label and per-phenomenon breakdown and adjudication logs; decisions on mapping Singlish phenomena to UD are described but not fully enumerated as formal guidelines in the paper.

Embedding preprocessing and selection of matched-size English corpus (Giga100M) are briefly described, but exact sampling, tokenization, and training parameters for embeddings are not fully documented, leaving domain/size confounds unresolved.

Jackknifing procedure for POS predictions used during parser training is described at a high level; code-level details (fold splits, random seeds, how predictions are integrated) are not included in the manuscript.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis is bounded by the materials provided in the manuscript excerpts and anonymized repository reference. Numerical summaries (e.g., some baseline numbers, full Table 4) were not fully present in the shared text, limiting precise verification of effect magnitudes. All reviewers consistently flagged limited sample sizes (test set 150 sentences; double-annotation 100 sentences) as the primary constraint on statistical confidence. Causal attribution between stacking, embedding choice, and training/initialization effects remains underdetermined without the requested ablations and resampling analyses. Finally, reproducibility cannot be confirmed until the public repository contains the enumerated artifacts (CoNLL-U, guidelines, scripts, seeds, licenses); the current assessment therefore treats reported improvements as plausible but provisional pending artifact and robustness disclosure.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript introduces a 1,200-sentence Universal Dependencies (UD) Singlish treebank and applies feature-level neural stacking (injecting English tagger/parser hidden features) together with in-domain ICE-SIN embeddings to improve POS tagging and dependency parsing on Singlish. Reported outcomes show substantive point improvements (POS up to 84.79%, parser UAS ~84.21%) and large reported relative error reductions versus Singlish-only baselines. The work pairs resource release, concrete UD mapping choices for Singlish phenomena, and per-phenomenon error analysis. Reviewers find the argument chain coherent and the approach plausible, but highlight several methodological and reporting gaps that limit confidence in effect magnitude and causal attribution.
strengths: Construction and UD-formatting of a Singlish dependency treebank (1,200 sentences, 10,986 words) with explicit mapping decisions for creole phenomena (topic-prominence, discourse particles, copula/NP deletion).

Coherent application of state-of-the-art components (bi-LSTM-CRF POS tagger; Dozat & Manning biaffine parser) and a documented feature-level neural stacking architecture adapted from prior work to perform cross-lingual transfer from English.
Empirical improvements reported for both POS tagging and parsing, plus per-grammar (phenomenon) error analysis that links annotation design to model behavior.
Commitment to public release of annotated data, code, and trained models (facilitates future validation and reuse).
limitations: Small evaluation and validation samples: held-out test set contains 150 sentences (~1,381 words) and inter-annotator agreement reported on only 100 sentences (aggregate UAS/LAS). This raises non-trivial uncertainty about the statistical stability of reported point improvements and generalizability across Singlish registers.

Insufficient causal isolation of components: ablation studies isolating the contribution of stacking vs in-domain embeddings vs simple capacity/initialization effects (e.g., tagger-only stacking, parser-only stacking, freezing vs fine-tuning English weights, matched-capacity baseline) are missing, leaving ambiguity about which design choices drive gains.

Embedding comparisons potentially confounded: ICE-SIN embeddings outperform English ones in reported conditions, but domain/register and preprocessing differences (ICE corpus spoken+written vs forum target; Giga100M selection details) are not fully controlled, so 'language-specific' interpretation is underdetermined.

Reproducibility and artifact completeness not yet verifiable: repository link in manuscript is anonymized and the paper does not (in the main text) include full annotation guidelines, adjudication logs, per-condition hyperparameters, random seeds, or bootstrap/CI computations.
open_questions: Please provide bootstrap confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics (or k-fold cross-validation) for POS accuracy, UAS and LAS so readers can assess variance and statistical significance of reported relative error reductions.

Please supply targeted ablations: (a) stack only POS emissions vs only parser MLP features, (b) run stacking with English components frozen vs fine-tuned, and (c) include a matched-parameter-count baseline (add comparable extra capacity without English features). Report POS/UAS/LAS per ablation.

Please release or attach the full annotation guidelines, adjudication protocol and logs, and per-label / per-phenomenon inter-annotator agreement (especially for discourse particles, topic-prominence, copula/NP deletion).

Please provide the public repository URL and an artifact manifest listing CoNLL-U files, training scripts/configs (including seeds), pre-trained embeddings used (or instructions to obtain them), and license/ethical notes on forum-derived data scraping and redistribution.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper builds and UD-annotates a 1,200-sentence Singlish treebank and applies feature-level neural stacking from English UD models plus in-domain ICE-SIN embeddings to improve POS tagging and dependency parsing. Point results show substantial improvements in POS accuracy and parser UAS relative to Singlish-only baselines; authors provide per-phenomenon error analyses and commit to releasing resources.

Strengths:
- Valuable resource creation: a UD-conformant Singlish treebank with explicit mapping rules for creole phenomena.
- Methodologically coherent: uses strong baseline architectures and a documented neural stacking transfer mechanism adapted from prior work.
- Empirical gains and diagnostic analyses: improvements reported for POS and parsing with per-grammar breakdowns that are useful diagnostically.
- Resource release commitment which, if complete, will enable community validation and reuse.

Limitations:
- Statistical stability: the held-out test set (150 sentences) and IAA sample (100 sentences) are small, and no confidence intervals or resampling statistics are reported; effect magnitudes may be sensitive to sampling variance.
- Attribution ambiguity: without ablations (tagger-only vs parser-only stacking, freezing vs fine-tuning English weights, matched-capacity control), it is unclear whether gains arise from transferred syntactic knowledge, improved lexical coverage, model capacity, or initialization effects.
- Embedding confounds: ICE-SIN's reported superiority may reflect domain/register/coverage differences or preprocessing choices rather than pure language-specific distributional benefits; controlled embedding comparisons are needed.
- Reproducibility gaps: repository link anonymized and manuscript lacks full guidelines, adjudication logs, hyperparameter manifests and seeds in the main text, preventing independent verification at present.

Open Questions:
- Can the authors provide bootstrap confidence intervals (or k-fold resampling) for POS/UAS/LAS and absolute error counts used for relative error reductions?
- Can the authors run and report ablations that isolate which stacked features drive gains (POS-only, parser-MLP-only), and experiments where English components are frozen versus fine-tuned, plus a matched-parameter-control baseline?
- Will the authors publish full annotation guidelines, per-label and per-phenomenon inter-annotator agreements, and adjudication logs for contentious cases (particularly discourse particles, topic-prominence, copula/NP deletion)?
- Please supply the public repository URL and an artifact manifest listing CoNLL-U files, scripts, configs, seeds, pretrained embeddings (or retrieval instructions), and the dataset license/ethics statement for forum-derived text.

Transparency:
The manuscript provides architecture descriptions and some hyperparameter choices and cites used implementations, which aids reproducibility in principle. However, several critical reproducibility items are missing or not verifiable in the draft: (1) anonymized repository link prevents artifact inspection; (2) no bootstrap/CIs or repeated-run stats reported; (3) full annotation guidelines, adjudication logs, and per-phenomenon IAA are absent; (4) embedding training/selection and jackknifing procedure details need fuller exposition. Release of the enumerated artifacts and additional robustness analyses will materially improve transparency and interpretability.

confidence_interval.rationale: Across reviewers there is moderate-to-high confidence that the approach (small UD treebank + neural stacking + in-domain embeddings) plausibly yields improvements over the small Singlish-only baseline; uncertainty lowers the estimate because of small test/IAA samples, lack of ablations and absent resampling statistics, and unverifiable release artifacts. Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones.
